questions.question: What does ACID stand for in database transactions?

options.text: Asynchronous, Concurrent, Isolated, Durable
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Automatic, Cached, Indexed, Distributed
Available, Consistent, Independent, Distributed

questions.explanation: ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives failures). These properties form the foundation of reliable database transactions. Banks, payment processors, and any system handling critical data rely on ACID guarantees. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, and Oracle all provide ACID compliance.

questions.question: What does Atomicity guarantee?

options.text: Transactions execute with minimal latency
All operations in a transaction succeed or all fail—no partial execution
Data is encrypted at the atomic level
Transactions can run in parallel without conflicts

questions.explanation: Atomicity ensures transactions are indivisible units. If any operation fails, all changes are rolled back to the previous state. A bank transfer either moves money completely or not at all—never deducts from one account without crediting another. Stripe relies on atomicity to ensure payment records are never in inconsistent states, even during failures.

questions.question: A transaction transfers $100 from Account A to Account B. Which ACID property ensures the total money in the system remains unchanged?

options.text: Atomicity - ensures both operations complete together
Consistency - ensures business rules are maintained
Isolation - ensures other transactions don't interfere
Durability - ensures the transfer is permanent

questions.explanation: Consistency ensures the database moves from one valid state to another, maintaining all defined rules and constraints. The business rule 'total money unchanged' is a consistency constraint. Atomicity ensures both debit and credit happen together; consistency ensures the result satisfies invariants. Database constraints, triggers, and application logic all contribute to consistency.

questions.question: Two transactions read the same row simultaneously. Which ACID property prevents them from seeing each other's uncommitted changes?

options.text: Atomicity - transactions are indivisible
Consistency - data remains valid
Isolation - concurrent transactions don't interfere
Durability - changes are permanent

questions.explanation: Isolation ensures concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot, unaffected by other uncommitted transactions. Without isolation, you might read data that gets rolled back (dirty read). PostgreSQL's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) provides isolation by maintaining multiple versions of rows.

questions.question: What does Durability guarantee?

options.text: Transactions complete within a time limit
Once committed, data survives system crashes and power failures
Data is replicated across multiple servers
Transactions can be undone after commit

questions.explanation: Durability ensures committed transactions are permanent—surviving crashes, power loss, and hardware failures. Achieved through write-ahead logging (WAL), flushing to disk before acknowledging commit, and replication. When your bank says 'transaction complete,' durability guarantees that money won't disappear if the server crashes a millisecond later.

questions.question: Which isolation levels exist in SQL databases? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Read Uncommitted
Read Committed
Repeatable Read
Serializable

questions.explanation: SQL defines four isolation levels (weakest to strongest): Read Uncommitted (dirty reads possible), Read Committed (no dirty reads—PostgreSQL default), Repeatable Read (no non-repeatable reads—MySQL InnoDB default), Serializable (full isolation, as if transactions ran sequentially). Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more locking and lower concurrency.

questions.question: What is a 'dirty read'?

options.text: Reading corrupted or malformed data
Reading uncommitted changes from another transaction
Reading old cached data instead of current values
Reading encrypted data without decryption

questions.explanation: Dirty read: Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before B commits. If B rolls back, A has read data that never officially existed—a phantom value. This can cause serious bugs in financial systems. Read Committed and higher isolation levels prevent dirty reads. Most production databases default to at least Read Committed for this reason.

questions.question: Why might an application choose a lower isolation level?

options.text: Lower isolation provides stronger security guarantees
Higher isolation reduces concurrency and performance
Lower isolation completely prevents all deadlocks
Lower isolation improves data durability

questions.explanation: Higher isolation requires more locking, reducing concurrency and throughput. Serializable isolation can reduce throughput by 10x or more compared to Read Committed. Applications may accept weaker isolation (e.g., Read Committed) for better performance when anomalies are rare or handled in application logic. Analytics workloads often use lower isolation since exact consistency matters less than query speed.

questions.question: True or False: NoSQL databases never support ACID transactions.

options.text: True - NoSQL sacrifices ACID for scalability
False - many NoSQL databases now support ACID

questions.explanation: Many NoSQL databases now support ACID: MongoDB (multi-document transactions since 4.0), DynamoDB (TransactWriteItems), CockroachDB (full ACID), FaunaDB, FoundationDB. The 'NoSQL = no ACID' assumption is outdated. Google Spanner proved you can have global scale AND ACID. Check specific database capabilities—the landscape has evolved significantly.

questions.question: What is a 'phantom read'?

options.text: Reading data that was deleted by another transaction
A query returns different rows on re-execution because another transaction inserted/deleted rows
Reading from a database that has crashed
Reading null values where data should exist

questions.explanation: Phantom read: Transaction A runs a query twice; between runs, Transaction B inserts or deletes rows matching A's WHERE clause. A sees different result sets—rows appear or disappear like phantoms. Only Serializable isolation prevents phantoms. This matters for reports or aggregations where consistent results are required across multiple queries in a transaction.

questions.question: How do databases typically implement durability?

options.text: Keeping all data in memory with battery backup
Write-ahead logging (WAL) and flushing to persistent storage
Compressing data to reduce storage requirements
Using faster CPUs for quicker transaction processing

questions.explanation: Durability uses Write-Ahead Logging: changes are written to a sequential log on disk before acknowledging commit. Even if the system crashes before data pages are written, the log allows recovery by replaying committed transactions. PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite all use WAL. Replication to other servers adds additional durability against hardware failures.

questions.question: A system requires high throughput for analytics queries that can tolerate slightly stale data. Which isolation level is most appropriate?

options.text: Serializable - ensures completely accurate results
Read Committed or Read Uncommitted for better throughput
Repeatable Read - balances accuracy and performance
Isolation level doesn't affect query throughput

questions.explanation: Analytics tolerating stale data can use lower isolation (Read Committed or even Read Uncommitted) for better throughput. Less locking means more concurrent queries. Data warehouses like Snowflake and BigQuery optimize for this pattern. Serializable would unnecessarily limit concurrency for workloads where perfect consistency isn't required. Match isolation level to business requirements.
